title: Streaming Data Fusion for the Internet of Things
problem: Semantically correct generation of rich feature vectors from multiple heterogeneous streaming data sources; the paper argues this had only been partially solved.
input_data: Heterogeneous IoT sensor streams plus weather forecasts and static/contextual data (energy; substation; train; smart lamp; traffic counter).
temporal_semantics: NO event-time vs availability-time distinction. Lookback offsets are raw array-index arithmetic assuming uniform ticks; on a detected timestamp misalignment the code logs an error and proceeds with the wrong row. Late-data policy is an inconsistent per-node-type monotonicity guard absent from three node types. Timezone/DST unspecified (host-local JS Date). Notably the paper itself observes that rare contributions discuss handling of delayed or out-of-sequence measurements - it names the gap without closing it. Source read at rev 708053a; see docs/original_system_audit.md.
generated_representation: Hand-authored JSON node/attribute configuration. Features are per-node lag offsets plus QMiner stream aggregates (ma/min/max/variance/EMA over declared windows). No generation - human-specified.
verification: None. Misalignment is logged not rejected; window boundary semantics are delegated to closed-source QMiner aggregates and untested in-repo; a written out-of-order test exists but is commented out.
datasets: Proprietary Slovenian deployments (smart meter; substation; train; smart lamp; traffic counter) plus Dark-Sky-shaped weather forecasts.
baselines: Data-driven models with vs without fused contextual and historical features.
metrics: Reported as significant improvement in accuracy of data-driven models applied to sensor streams; specific metrics not given.
limitations: Stated contributions are a formal definition of heterogeneous stream fusion; the first generic feature-vector framework for heterogeneous streams; and a real-world edge/cloud architecture. The temporal defects above are audit findings the paper does not state.
relationship_to_this_work: DIRECT PREDECESSOR and the source of the M2 expert baseline. Its formal definition specifies WHAT to compute and never WHEN a value is knowable - which is exactly the axis this work adds. It named delayed and out-of-sequence measurement handling as a rare open problem and then did not solve it in its own engine. This work keeps the fusion problem and replaces the temporal foundation; features move from human-authored to LLM-proposed and machine-verified.

title: Large Language Models for Automated Data Science: Introducing CAAFE for Context-Aware Automated Feature Engineering
problem: Incorporating domain knowledge into AutoML by having an LLM generate semantically meaningful features from natural-language dataset descriptions.
input_data: Tabular datasets with dataset descriptions (pandas DataFrames preloaded for code execution).
temporal_semantics: Not addressed - i.i.d. tabular. Acceptance is measured over TEN RANDOM validation splits; there is no prediction time in the method; so nothing in it could detect temporal leakage.
generated_representation: Python code creating new features plus natural-language explanations of utility. LLM is also instructed to drop redundant features.
verification: Syntax of generated Python is parsed against a WHITELIST of allowed operations; imports and arbitrary function calls are excluded. The paper states this does not provide full security and does not exclude infinite loops or excessive resource usage. No type; unit; state-bound; or temporal checking.
feedback_loop: Yes - two loops. Execution errors are passed back to the LLM for the next iteration (the paper reports recovering from all errors this way); and a feature is kept only if the mean of accuracy and ROC AUC change over ten random validation splits is greater than zero; otherwise rejected.
datasets: 14 tabular datasets in the main evaluation; deliberately split into OpenML sets released before the LLM knowledge cutoff and Kaggle sets released after it as a contamination control.
baselines: Logistic regression; random forest; TabPFN; plus DFS and AutoFeat (context-agnostic AutoFE) alone and combined with CAAFE.
metrics: ROC AUC - mean 0.798 to 0.822 across datasets.
limitations: Acknowledges LLM code-execution risk; benchmark contamination risk; and (per the repo) bias replication and API cost.
relationship_to_this_work: CLOSEST ON THE GENERATE-EXECUTE-VALIDATE LOOP and a direct competitor on the primary dataset - OCTree Table 13 reports CAAFE improving Enefit by only 0.4 percent over XGBoost. Its safety mechanism is a syntax whitelist over arbitrary Python that the authors themselves call incomplete; this work makes ineligible dependencies unrepresentable in a restricted DSL instead of filtering dangerous Python. Its acceptance criterion is random-split validation gain; this work accepts under chronological replay with recorded availability. Its pre/post-cutoff dataset split is a contamination-control precedent worth adopting in Phase 8.

title: Optimized Feature Generation for Tabular Data via LLMs with Decision Tree Reasoning
problem: Automated feature engineering without a manually specified search space and without relying solely on validation scores for selection.
input_data: Tabular data; including two time-series-derived regression tasks (Tesla stock; Enefit).
temporal_semantics: Partially addressed at the SPLIT level only: the two time-series tabular regression tasks are split by time index rather than randomly; all other datasets use three random splits. Within a row there is no temporal structure - Enefit is flattened to static columns (Prediction Unit Id; Day; Hour; prices; installed capacity; local forecast weather) discarding data_block_id and any issue-time vs valid-time distinction. No availability time; no late data; no leakage checking.
generated_representation: Natural-language feature generation RULES produced by the LLM; a new column is materialised from each rule. Decision trees (CART) fitted to the training data are verbalised as reasoning feedback.
verification: None beyond validation score. Step 4 is explicitly select the rule with the best validation score. No correctness; safety; type; unit; or temporal checking is described.
feedback_loop: Yes - the LLM receives both the validation score and a natural-language rendering of a CART decision tree fitted to the data including the new feature; iterated a fixed number of times.
datasets: Disease; Academic; Enefit; Tesla Stock (Kaggle); Clinical Trial (US NLM); plus the 19 anonymised classification datasets of Grinsztajn et al.
baselines: XGBoost; MLP; HyperFast baselines without feature engineering; and CAAFE (Table 13).
metrics: Test error rate percent for classification; MAE x10^-3 for regression; mean and standard deviation over three splits.
limitations: Not stated as a limitations section. Enefit gains are marginal - 2.3 percent with GPT-4o and 0.0 percent with Llama 2 on XGBoost.
relationship_to_this_work: SINGLE CLOSEST COMPETITOR - it is LLM feature generation evaluated on Enefit; this project's primary dataset; with chronological splits. Two gaps define the contrast. First it flattens Enefit into static tabular rows; discarding exactly the release-block and forecast-revision structure that makes the dataset a temporal benchmark; so its time-index split controls the train/test boundary but nothing inside a row. Second selection is by validation score alone with no correctness check of any kind. Its Enefit result (2.3 percent with GPT-4o; 0.0 percent with Llama 2) is simultaneously the bar H1 must clear and a warning that the dataset resists naive feature generation.

title: LLM-FE: Automated Feature Engineering for Tabular Data with LLMs as Evolutionary Optimizers
venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research; arXiv v1 Mar 2025
problem: Pre-defined AutoFE search spaces; and LLM methods that use direct prompting or validation scores alone and so fail to reuse insight from prior feature-discovery experiments.
input_data: Tabular data - 19 classification and 10 regression datasets.
temporal_semantics: Not addressed. Split is a sub-training/validation partition of the training data with no time ordering.
generated_representation: Feature transformation PROGRAMS (Python functions mapping data_in to data_out); the task is formulated explicitly as program search over an evolutionary population with island-based memory.
verification: Execute-and-discard only. Each sampled program is executed before evaluation to discard error-prone programs; and a maximum execution-time threshold discards slow ones. This is runtime filtering rather than verification - nothing establishes type; unit; state-bound; or temporal correctness; and a program that leaks executes perfectly well.
feedback_loop: Yes - evolutionary search where high-scoring programs are retained in island memory and resampled as in-context demonstrations; validation score is the fitness signal.
datasets: 19 classification and 10 regression tabular datasets following the CAAFE selection.
baselines: OpenFE; AutoFeat (non-LLM); CAAFE; FeatLLM; OCTree; and the raw-data base model. Predictors XGBoost (default); MLP; TabPFN. Backbones GPT-3.5-Turbo and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
metrics: Mean rank across datasets; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests in the appendix.
limitations: Future work names domain-specific LLMs and extension to cleaning/imputation/tuning. No temporal or correctness limitation is acknowledged.
relationship_to_this_work: STRONGEST CURRENT AutoFE-AS-PROGRAM-SEARCH BASELINE and the nearest methodological neighbour to the M8 proposal loop. Its notion of a valid program is one that runs without raising inside a time limit; this work replaces that with a compiler that proves or rejects type; unit; lineage; state-bound; and temporal eligibility before execution. Methodologically important: it equalises all LLM baselines on a fixed budget of 20 LLM SAMPLES - precisely the axis section 9.4 rejects as handing the LLM method a hidden compute advantage - whereas this work equalises on candidate evaluations and reports LLM calls as overhead. It also explicitly prompts the LLM to generate complex features to counteract the Kuken bias.

title: Large Language Models Engineer Too Many Simple Features For Tabular Data
problem: Whether LLMs exhibit a systematic operator-selection bias when engineering features; and whether that bias costs predictive performance.
generated_representation: Engineered features derived from LLM-suggested operators applied to existing columns.
verification: Not a verification paper. The instrument is a comparison of the LLM operator-frequency distribution against the frequencies obtained by black-box search with OpenFE; treated as the reference for optimal operator use.
datasets: 27 tabular classification datasets selected to be unknown to all evaluated LLMs.
baselines: Four LLMs - GPT-4o-mini; Gemini-1.5-flash; Llama3.1-8B; Mistral7B-v0.3 - plus GPT-4o in a further experiment; with OpenFE black-box search as the operator reference.
metrics: Operator frequency distribution anomalies; and downstream predictive performance.
limitations: Scope is tabular classification and the operator vocabulary of OpenFE.
relationship_to_this_work: NOT A COMPETING METHOD BUT THE EMPIRICAL WARRANT FOR TWO DESIGN CHOICES. It shows LLMs over-select simple operators such as Add and under-use compositional ones such as GroupByThenMean relative to black-box search; and that this costs accuracy. That is direct evidence M3 will be a strong baseline and that H1 is a genuine test rather than a formality; and it justifies reporting the operator-frequency distribution of accepted features as a diagnostic. Its selection of datasets unknown to the LLMs is a second contamination-control precedent.

title: FeatEHR-LLM: Leveraging Large Language Models for Feature Engineering in Electronic Health Records
problem: Feature engineering over irregularly sampled EHR time series with variable measurement frequencies and structural sparsity; where existing methods lack clinical awareness or assume clean inputs.
input_data: Irregularly sampled clinical time series. The LLM sees only dataset schemas and task descriptions - never raw patient records - as a privacy control.
temporal_semantics: THE CLOSEST TEMPORAL HANDLING IN THE READING LIST; but it solves irregularity rather than eligibility. A tool-augmented mechanism gives the LLM specialised routines for querying irregular temporal data so generated code handles uneven observation patterns and informative sparsity within a fixed task-specific horizon. Everything inside the observation window is assumed knowable: no availability time; no forecast issue/valid time; no late-arriving data; no leakage check.
generated_representation: Executable feature-extraction code for univariate and multivariate features; generated in multiple rounds.
verification: Syntax and runtime verification in a feature-to-code translation pipeline - i.e. it parses and it runs. Plus in-loop validation on predictive performance. No semantic or temporal correctness checking.
feedback_loop: Yes - iterative multi-round generation with in-loop validation driving refinement.
datasets: Eight clinical prediction tasks across four ICU datasets.
baselines: Strong baselines (not enumerated in the abstract or conclusion).
metrics: AUROC - highest mean on 7 of 8 tasks; up to 6 percentage points improvement.
limitations: States risk of LLM hallucination in generated feature logic; and absence of explicit missing-data mechanism modelling (MCAR/MAR/MNAR); both warranting expert review before clinical deployment. Also notes redundancy among generated features.
relationship_to_this_work: CLOSEST TEMPORAL COMPETITOR and the paper whose framing most resembles this one - schema-and-task-description prompting rather than raw data; executable generated code; tool support for awkward time structure. The distinction is which temporal problem is solved: FeatEHR handles IRREGULAR SAMPLING inside a fixed horizon while assuming everything in the window is knowable; this work handles ELIGIBILITY - what was knowable at prediction time - which is orthogonal and remains unaddressed there. Its verification is syntax plus successful execution; ours is a compiler over a restricted DSL. Its schema-only prompting independently validates this project's metadata-only proposal interface.

title: Flash-Fusion: Enabling Expressive Low-Latency Queries on IoT Sensor Streams with LLMs
problem: The IoT data collection and analysis burden - terabytes of low-level readings; and analysis that requires iterative effort and technical expertise.
input_data: IoT sensor streams; evaluated on university bus fleet telemetry (accelerometer; GPS).
temporal_semantics: Edge-side fixed-window statistical summarisation (mean/variance of acceleration magnitude; high-percentile axes; GPS and time context) chosen as lossy compression for cost rather than as a semantics. No availability time; no eligibility; no leakage concept.
generated_representation: Cloud-based query plans - behavioural clustering plus context-rich prompt assembly. Produces answers to natural-language questions; NOT features for a downstream predictor.
verification: None in the correctness sense. Quality is judged as factual consistency of responses relative to a raw-data baseline.
datasets: University bus fleet deployment; proprietary; no public dataset.
baselines: Feeding raw IoT telemetry directly to a state-of-the-art LLM (Llama 3.1 8B).
metrics: 95 percent latency reduction; 98 percent token/cost reduction; 73.5 percent data reduction from edge summarisation.
limitations: Under review; scalability and architectural limits not detailed.
relationship_to_this_work: SHARES THE IoT-STREAM SUBSTRATE AND LITTLE ELSE. The LLM answers questions about telemetry rather than constructing features that a model will train on; so no notion of prediction time or leakage arises. Useful as evidence that LLMs over IoT streams is an active area a reviewer will know about; and as a clean contrast - expressive querying of past data versus verified construction of features for future prediction. Its edge summarisation is a cost optimisation; this work's windowing is a semantics that must be provably eligible.

title: Empowering Time Series Forecasting with LLM-Agents (DCATS)
problem: Argues that for time series forecasting - where lightweight models already reach state of the art - improving DATA QUALITY is a more productive AutoML axis than model architecture search.
input_data: Time series; large-scale traffic volume forecasting.
temporal_semantics: Not addressed. Data selection reasons about proximate and pattern-similar locations; not about when data became available.
generated_representation: A data selection and enrichment plan - which auxiliary series to include - iteratively refined; not feature programs.
feedback_loop: Yes - the agent evaluates the impact of different enrichment strategies and refines the selection plan.
datasets: A large-scale traffic volume forecasting dataset.
relationship_to_this_work: CLOSEST ON LLM AGENT PLUS TIME SERIES but it operates on data SELECTION and cleaning rather than feature construction; and optimises forecast error directly with no verification and no availability semantics. It confirms the data-centric LLM framing is live and worth citing; it does not contest any contribution claimed here. Its enrichment-from-related-series idea overlaps this project's declared entity graph and is worth citing there.

title: Feast documentation: point-in-time joins
problem: Reproducing feature state at a past point in time when building training datasets; so a model does not learn from values unavailable at inference.
input_data: Feature views joined against an entity dataframe carrying timestamps.
temporal_semantics: TWO DISTINCT TIMESTAMPS - event timestamp (when the event occurred; the join scans backward from the entity timestamp up to a TTL) and created timestamp (when the value was written or backfilled; used to deduplicate rows sharing an event timestamp - highest created wins). Setting filter_by_created_timestamp=True adds created_timestamp <= entity_timestamp so backfilled values cannot leak into training data. This is the industry precedent closest to the event_time/available_time distinction.
generated_representation: Not applicable - no generation; declarative feature view definitions.
verification: Not applicable - correctness is a property of the join the user opts into; nothing is verified. Offline stores lacking support raise rather than silently ignoring the flag.
limitations: Leak prevention is OFF BY DEFAULT - the default join filters on event timestamp only. Not all offline stores support the flag; rows with NULL created timestamp are dropped when it is enabled; scope is offline historical retrieval.
relationship_to_this_work: THE MOST SERIOUS CHALLENGE TO CONTRIBUTION 1; and it comes from infrastructure rather than research. The event/created timestamp pair IS recognisably the event_time/available_time distinction and it exists precisely to stop backfilled values leaking. Three defensible differences: it is an opt-in RETRIEVAL discipline (off by default) rather than a property of a computation; there is no generation and no compiler; so nothing checks a proposed feature; and it has no concept of forecast issue time; valid time; or revision. The honest claim is therefore NOT that the availability distinction is new - it must not be claimed as new - but that verifying it over generated streaming feature programs is.

title: River documentation: progressive_val_score (delayed progressive validation)
problem: Evaluating online and streaming models as they would actually have performed in production; where ground truth arrives after a lag.
input_data: Streaming samples each carrying a moment (timestamp) and subject to a delay.
temporal_semantics: The model predicts each observation before being updated on it; the target is revealed only after the delay parameter; which may be a constant; an integer; a timedelta; a feature field name; or a callable over features and target; and must be arithmetically compatible with moment.
verification: Not applicable - an evaluation protocol; not a verifier.
feedback_loop: Not applicable in the feature-generation sense.
baselines: Contrasted with cross-validation; which does not respect ordering.
limitations: Without a delay samples are processed one after another; which does not capture realistic feedback lag.
relationship_to_this_work: DIRECT PRECEDENT FOR THE EVALUATION PROTOCOL - to be adopted and cited; not contested. Delayed progressive validation is the delayed-label discipline Phase 6 requires; and River is already a planned dependency. That per-sample delayed evaluation is standard practice STRENGTHENS this work rather than weakening it: the contribution is not the evaluation loop but what is proven about a feature program before it is allowed into that loop. Do not claim novelty for delayed prequential evaluation.

title: Chronos-2: From Univariate to Universal Forecasting
problem: Existing pretrained forecasters are largely univariate; limiting applicability where multivariate data and covariates matter. OPTIONAL comparison per research plan section 4.
input_data: Univariate; multivariate; and covariate-informed time series.
temporal_semantics: Not addressed - no availability-time or leakage handling stated.
generated_representation: Not applicable - a pretrained forecasting model rather than a feature generator; group attention shares information across series; targets; and covariates. Zero-shot inference.
datasets: fev-bench; GIFT-Eval; Chronos Benchmark II; plus energy and retail case studies.
baselines: Existing pretrained and zero-shot forecasting models.
relationship_to_this_work: NOT A FEATURE-ENGINEERING METHOD; relevant in two ways only. As an optional strong external comparator for RQ1 on the forecasting tasks; and as a scope boundary - section 2.3 excludes using a general-purpose LLM as the numerical forecaster; and Chronos-2 is what that excluded approach looks like done well. If it beats the full pipeline on some tasks that is a limitation to report honestly; it would not refute H2a or H2b; which are correctness claims.
